stemBlocks.value: O is the origin, OX = u and OY = v. OX and OY are extended so that X and Y are the midpoints of OA and OB respectively. (i) Express BX in terms of u and v. (ii) YA and BX intersect at M with BM = 2MX. (a) Express BM in terms of u and v. (b) Use a vector method to establish the ratio in which M divides YA.
Think first: Because X and Y are midpoints, OA = 2u and OB = 2v — write those down first, and every other vector follows.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p284-q07 from workbook page 284.

solutionSteps.instruction: Use the midpoint information to write OA and OB.

contentBlocks.value: X is the midpoint of OA, so OA = 2 OX; Y is the midpoint of OB, so OB = 2 OY

solutionSteps.instruction: Find BX by subtracting the position vectors of B and X.
Convert BM = 2MX into a fraction of BX. It means BM : MX = 2 : 1, so BM is two-thirds of BX.
Add BM to OB to reach M.
Find YM and YA and compare them.

contentBlocks.value: YM = OM − OY = (2/3)u − (1/3)v; YA = OA − OY = 2u − v; so YM = (1/3)(2u − v)

solutionSteps.instruction: Read off the division of YA. Since YM is one third of the whole of YA, the remaining part MA is two thirds.

contentBlocks.value: Result: M divides YA with YM : YA = 1 : 3, i.e. YM : MA = 1 : 2

strategyBlocks.value: Use OA = 2u and OB = 2v, build BX by subtraction, take two-thirds of it for BM, add to OB to get the position vector of M, then compare YM with YA.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (i) BX = u − 2v  (ii)(a) BM = (2/3)(u − 2v) = (2/3)u − (4/3)v  (b) OM = (2/3)u + (2/3)v, so YM = (2/3)u − (1/3)v = (1/3)(2u − v) = (1/3)YA. M therefore lies on YA with YM equal to one third of the whole line YA, that is YM : YA = 1 : 3 and YM : MA = 1 : 2.

whyThisWorks.value: The midpoint conditions double u and v to reach A and B, so every point in the figure can be written with just those two vectors. Splitting BX in the ratio 2 : 1 fixes M as a single point, and its position vector then lets you test whether M lies on YA: because YM comes out as a pure scalar multiple of YA, M is on that line and the scalar is exactly the fraction of YA covered. Note carefully whether a ratio compares a part to the whole (YM : YA) or a part to the remaining part (YM : MA) — they are different statements of the same fact.

commonErrors.misconception: Taking BM = (1/2)BX instead of (2/3)BX from BM = 2MX.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Taking BM = (1/2)BX instead of (2/3)BX from BM = 2MX.

commonErrors.misconception: Writing BX = 2v − u by reversing the direction.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Writing BX = 2v − u by reversing the direction.

commonErrors.misconception: Confusing the part-to-whole ratio YM : YA = 1 : 3 with the part-to-part ratio YM : MA = 1 : 2.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Confusing the part-to-whole ratio YM : YA = 1 : 3 with the part-to-part ratio YM : MA = 1 : 2.

commonErrors.misconception: Forgetting that X and Y are midpoints and using OA = u, OB = v.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Forgetting that X and Y are midpoints and using OA = u, OB = v.

examTip.value: After finding a point's position vector, always test collinearity by writing one vector as a multiple of another — the multiple itself tells you the ratio.
